## Sarek 3.1.1 Optimization

nf-core/sarek 3.1.1 is a complete re-implementation of the pipeline utilizing the Nextflow DSL2 framework [15][19]. This architectural shift enables modularization and code sharing, with 78 of the 80 modules used in the pipeline being sourced from the nf-core community's shared repository [5]. This modular design makes the code base more maintainable and allows for "drop-in" replacements of tools [16]. Additionally, the use of modular configuration files allows users to customize command-line arguments at runtime without modifying the underlying code [16]. Portability and reproducibility are ensured by using individual containers (Docker or Singularity) for each module [5].

To optimize performance and storage, the pipeline transitioned from using BAM files to the CRAM format for intermediate data storage [1][8]. This change, combined with reducing the amount of scattering, enables the pipeline to run more efficiently on smaller compute systems [4]. Specifically, the switch to CRAM reduced pre-processing storage requirements by 65%, dropping from 170.4 TB to 59.7 TB in benchmark tests [12]. Methodological improvements also include the integration of fastP, which accelerates computation by combining FastQ sharding and adapter trimming into a single step [8]. Furthermore, the pipeline now supports increased intra-sample parallelization through scatter-gathering across intervals for all applicable variant calling tools [10][19][26].

These optimizations have resulted in a significant reduction in compute costs, showing a 69% to 70% decrease compared to version 2.7.2 [5][14][19][22]. On AWS Batch, the average cost for analyzing a single normal sample was reduced from $68.04 to $20.82 [4][24]. Performance metrics indicate an 84% reduction in runtime and a 70% reduction in required CPU hours for single-sample analysis [13][18]. These improvements allow for comprehensive germline short and structural variant calling and annotation to be completed for approximately $20 per sample [5][14][22].

## Sarek Baseline and Evolution

Sarek is an open-source, portable workflow designed for the analysis of germline and somatic variants using data from whole-genome sequencing (WGS), whole-exome sequencing (WES), or gene panels [2][5]. The primary goals of the software include providing easy installation, robust portability across different compute environments, comprehensive documentation, transparent and easy-to-read code, and extensive quality metrics reporting [2][5]. It is built to serve as both a production-grade workflow for sequencing facilities and a stand-alone tool for individual research groups [4][5].

The architecture of Sarek is implemented in the Nextflow workflow language, which allows the code to be easily adjusted and extended while offering native support for various execution environments like Slurm and cloud platforms such as AWS [7]. To ensure reproducibility and ease of deployment, Sarek utilizes Docker and Singularity containers as well as Conda environments, enabling it to run on any POSIX-compatible system [2][7][9]. This design is specifically intended to support compute environments that handle sensitive personal data, even those without direct internet access [5][7].

Sarek follows GATK best-practice recommendations for its initial processing stages, which include read alignment using BWA-MEM followed by deduplication and recalibration via GATK [4][6][9]. For variant calling, the workflow integrates several state-of-the-art tools:
*   **Germline variants:** HaplotypeCaller, Strelka2, Manta, and TIDDIT [6][9].
*   **Somatic mutations:** Mutect2, Strelka2, and Freebayes [6][9][10].
*   **Structural variants and ploidy:** Manta, ASCAT, and Control-FREEC [6][9][10].

Functional annotation of variants is performed using snpEff and VEP [6][10]. The workflow also generates extensive quality control metrics using tools like FastQC, QualiMap, and Samtools, which are aggregated into a single report via MultiQC [6][10]. To optimize performance, Sarek employs a scatter-gather approach, dividing the genome into smaller chunks to distribute processing across multiple CPU cores [9].

## Clinical History and Brucellosis Seropositivity

Clinical history, particularly reproductive complications, is strongly associated with brucellosis seropositivity in livestock in the Somali pastoral region of Ethiopia [1][2][5]. In small ruminants (sheep and goats), a history of retained fetal membranes (RFM) is a significant risk factor, with 33.3% of affected animals testing positive for *Brucella* spp. [3][25]. Multivariable analysis indicates that small ruminants with a history of RFM are between 8.2 times (OR: 8.2, 95% CI: 2.4–29) and 9 times (OR: 9, 95% CI: 1.9–42) more likely to be seropositive than those without such a history [2][3][23][25]. Additionally, sheep and goats with a history of abortion had a seroprevalence of 23% (OR: 3, 95% CI: 0.9–9.7), though this was not statistically significant in the final multivariable model [3][25]. Herd size also influenced results; animals in large flocks (>50) were 5.01 times more likely to acquire the infection (OR: 5.01, 95% CI: 1.2–21.4) compared to those in small herds [2][3][7][22][23][25].

In camels, reproductive clinical history is also a primary indicator of infection [2][13]. Camels with a history of RFM showed a seroprevalence of 35.7% [9][17][26]. Univariable analysis for camels showed a significant association with RFM (OR: 22, 95% CI: 5.9–8), while the final multivariable model found an even stronger association (OR: 35, 95% CI: 12.7–60) [2][9][10][23][26]. A history of abortion in camels was associated with a 10.2% seroprevalence and an OR of 3.9 (95% CI: 1.2–13) [2][9][17][23]. Furthermore, physiological status was a factor; pregnant camels had a 9.8% seroprevalence and were significantly more likely to be seropositive (OR: 3.3, 95% CI: 1.4–15) [2][9][17][23].

These associations exist because *Brucella* spp. target reproductive organs, causing inflammation of the uterine wall (metritis), which leads to abortion and the subsequent retention of fetal membranes [4][14][18].

## Pastoralist Knowledge and Clinical Observations

Brucellosis is considered one of the top five prioritized zoonotic diseases in Ethiopia, with animal brucellosis first reported in the country during the 1970s [1]. Seroepidemiological studies conducted across various regions of Ethiopia have reported a prevalence range between 1.5% and 22.2% [1]. The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) estimates that annual economic losses in livestock production due to the disease range from USD 200 to 600 million [1]. 

The study conducted in the Goro Baqaqsa, Guradamole, and Dolo Ado districts of the Liban Zone aimed to assess the knowledge, attitude, and exposure risks of Somali pastoralist herders toward brucellosis [1]. question: Describe the laboratory diagnostic sequence and the statistical methods used to identify significant risk factors for brucellosis in this study.
step_result_content:
## Laboratory Diagnostic Sequence

The laboratory diagnostic sequence for brucellosis begins with the collection of blood samples via venipuncture: 10 mL from the jugular veins of camels, 4–5 mL from the jugular veins of sheep and goats, and approximately 5 mL from the medium cuboidal vein in humans [2]. These samples are labeled and left tilted overnight at room temperature to allow for clotting, after which the sera are decanted into sterile cryovials [2]. The samples are transported in an ice box and stored at −20°C for processing [2].

The initial screening is performed using the Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT) [2]. For camels, 30 μL of RBPT is used, while for sheep and goats, the test uses one volume of antigen to three volumes of serum (e.g., 25 μL to 75 μL) to improve sensitivity [3]. The antigen and serum are mixed with a plastic applicator for four minutes, and results are read immediately based on the presence and level of agglutination (weak, moderate, or strong) [3]. Both positive and negative control sera are used for interpretation [3].

All samples that test positive during the RBPT screening are subjected to further confirmatory testing [3]. Animal sera are tested using a commercial competitive ELISA (cELISA), while human sera are tested using an IgG ELISA, following the manufacturer’s protocols [3]. A sample is defined as seropositive only if it tests positive for both the RBPT and ELISA methods [3].

## Statistical Methods

To identify risk factors for brucellosis, the study employed both univariable and multivariable logistic regression analyses [1][2][3][6]. These statistical methods were used to calculate Odds Ratios (OR), 95% Confidence Intervals (CI), and p-values to determine the strength and significance of associations between various variables and *Brucella* spp. seropositivity [1][3][4][6]. 

The diagnostic process used to define seropositivity for these analyses involved a serial testing approach to minimize false positives [1]. The Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT) served as a high-sensitivity screening tool, while a competitive Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay (c-ELISA) was used for its high specificity to confirm results [1]. For sheep and goats, a modified mRBPT was utilized alongside c-ELISA [1].

In humans, univariable regression was used to assess factors such as age, gender, and the presence of seropositive animals in the household [6]. Multivariable logistic regression was further applied to evaluate behavioral risks, such as raw milk consumption, assisting with calving, and the disposal of aborted fetal materials [1][3]. For livestock, multivariable logistic regression analyzed factors including flock or herd size, history of abortion, parity, and the presence of retained fetal membranes (RFM) to identify significant predictors of infection [2][4][5].

## Risk Factors Considered

The study evaluated several potential risk factors. For animals, these included: Herd size (large herd size), Herd history of retained fetal membranes (RFM), Pregnancy, History of abortion, Livestock management practices, Animal movements and migration, Environmental factors, Pastoralist behaviors and practices, Lack of veterinary control measures, Socioeconomic factors, Genetic content of the animal host population, Biology of Brucella spp., Age, Sex, Species, Parity, Physiological status. For humans, factors included: Disposing of or contact with retained fetal membranes (RFM), Handling of infected animals, Ingestion of contaminated animal products (unpasteurized milk and milk products, meat), Assisting animals during calving or birthing, Close contact with infected animals / Presence of seropositive animals in the household, Sex (higher seroprevalence observed in females).

## Significant Risk Factors and Statistical Results

The study conducted in the Somali Pastoral region of Eastern Ethiopia identified several significant risk factors for Brucella spp. seropositivity in livestock and humans [8]. The overall seroprevalence was found to be 5% in small ruminants, 2.9% in camels, and 2.0% in humans [3][8].

**Animal Risk Factors**
For small ruminants (sheep and goats), significant risk factors in the multivariable analysis included:
*   **Large flock size:** Animals in large flocks were 5.01 times more likely to be seropositive compared to those in small flocks (OR = 5.01, 95% CI: 1.2–21.4, p = 0.02) [4][5][9].
*   **History of Retained Fetal Membranes (RFM):** This was strongly associated with seropositivity (OR = 8.2, 95% CI: 2.4–29, p = 0.00) [5][9].

For camels, the primary significant risk factor identified in multivariable regression was:
*   **History of RFM:** Camels with a history of RFM had significantly higher odds of seropositivity (OR = 35, 95% CI: 12.7–60, p = 0.004) [4][11]. 
*   **Univariable findings:** Prior to multivariable adjustment, pregnancy (OR = 3.3, 95% CI: 1.4–15, p < 0.05) and a history of abortion (OR = 3.9, 95% CI: 1.2–13, p < 0.05) were also significant [4][10]. Female camels generally showed higher seroprevalence (4%) than males (0.7%) [13].

**Human Risk Factors**
The most significant risk factor for human seropositivity was related to animal handling:
*   **Disposal of Retained Fetal Membranes:** Handling and disposing of aborted fetal materials or RFM was significantly associated with infection. Multivariable analysis showed an OR of 37.4 (95% CI: 5.1–18.5, p = 0.001) [7], while univariable analysis showed an OR of 26 (95% CI: 4.0–45.6, p = 0.001) [1][12].

Other factors investigated but found **not** to be statistically significant included:
*   **Raw milk consumption:** Participants consuming raw milk had higher odds of seropositivity, but it was not significant (OR = 5.7, 95% CI: 0.9–35, p = 0.06) [1][12].
*   **Assisting during calving/birthing:** This practice showed higher odds but lacked statistical significance (Multivariable OR = 8, 95% CI: 0.6–127, p = 0.11 [7]; Univariable OR = 3.6, 95% CI: 0.58–22, p = 0.16 [1]).
*   **Household contact:** Living in a household with seropositive animals increased the risk by seven times, yet remained statistically non-significant (OR = 7, 95% CI: 0.2–13.7, p = 0.72) [1][12].

## Serial Testing and Case Definition

Based on the provided documents, the serial testing approach used in this study and its relationship to the statistical definition of a "positive" case can be explained as follows:

### 1. The Serial Testing Approach
The study employed a two-stage testing strategy to identify *Brucella* antibodies in humans, camels, sheep, and goats. This approach is designed to balance sensitivity and specificity.

*   **Step 1: Screening (RBPT):** All samples were first screened using the **Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT)**. This test was chosen for its **high sensitivity**, meaning it is effective at catching as many potential cases as possible. To further enhance sensitivity in sheep and goats, the researchers used a modified RBPT (one volume of antigen to three volumes of serum).
*   **Step 2: Confirmation (cELISA/IgG ELISA):** Only samples that tested positive during the RBPT screening were subjected to a second test. Animal samples were tested using a **Competitive ELISA (cELISA)**, while human samples were tested using an **IgG ELISA**. These tests were selected for their **high specificity**, which helps exclude false-positive results caused by cross-reactions with other bacteria.

### 2. Statistical Definition of a 'Positive' Case
The study utilized a strict case definition to ensure the accuracy of the findings, particularly because vaccination is not practiced in Ethiopia (meaning any positive result indicates natural infection):

*   **Individual Seropositivity:** An individual (human or animal) was only recorded as "seropositive" if the sample tested **positive on both tests** (RBPT and ELISA). If a sample was positive on the RBPT but negative on the ELISA, it was not considered a positive case.
*   **Flock/Herd Seropositivity:** A flock or herd was defined as seropositive if **at least one animal** within that group tested positive for both tests.

### 3. Rationale for this Approach
The primary goal of using this serial method was to **rule out false-positive cross-reactions** and maintain "maximal specificity." By requiring a sample to pass two different types of tests, the researchers ensured that the reported prevalence (overall 5% across the study) was a reliable reflection of actual *Brucella* infection within the Somali pastoralist communities and their livestock.

question: Compare the diagnostic methodologies and biological markers used to determine the prevalence of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) and Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) as described in studies from Cameroon and Ethiopia.

## PPR Ethiopia: Diagnostics and Markers

To determine the prevalence of Peste des petits ruminants (PPR) in Ethiopia, researchers employed a combination of active cross-sectional studies and retrospective epidemiological analyses [2][6]. The primary diagnostic methodology for estimating seroprevalence was the competition enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (c-ELISA) [2]. *   **Sample Negativity Percentage (S/N%):** OD values were converted into S/N% to determine status; samples with an S/N% of 50% or less were classified as positive, while those above 60% were negative [9].
*   **Clinical Indicators:** Though the prevalence study focused on serology, clinical markers of the disease were identified as pyrexia, nasal and ocular discharge, breathing difficulties, and erosive alterations or necrosis in the mucosal lining of the digestive system [4].
*   **Age Determination:** The age of study animals was determined based on dentition [6].

question: What is the specific purpose of the regularized logarithm (rlog) transformation, and how does its performance compare to an ordinary log transformation in terms of variance stabilization?
step_result_content:
## rlog Transformation Analysis

The purpose of the rlog transformation is to make count data homoskedastic, ensuring that the variance does not depend strongly on the mean counts [1]. By providing variables with a similar dynamic range, it facilitates multivariate visualizations and ordinations, such as clustering or principal component analysis [1]. The transformation accounts for variations in sequencing depth (size factors) across samples [2]. It is important to note that the rlog transformation is intended for visualization and ordination purposes; it is distinct from the statistical inference procedure used for differential expression analysis, which utilizes raw counts [1][2].

In terms of performance regarding variance stabilization, the rlog transformation outperforms the ordinary logarithm (specifically the logarithm of normalized counts plus a pseudocount) [3]. Diagnostic plots show that while the ordinary logarithm results in gene-wise standard deviations that are variable across the range of mean counts, the rlog transformation keeps the variance relatively stable [3]. This stabilization helps reveal meaningful patterns in the data [3]. For example, in the Hammer et al. dataset, hierarchical clustering using ordinary logarithm-transformed counts produced ambiguous results, whereas the rlog-transformed data successfully clustered samples into groups defined by treatment and time [3].

## Technical Details of rlog

Calculation: The rlog transformation is calculated by fitting a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) for each gene with a baseline expression (intercept only). For each sample, shrunken Log Fold Changes (LFCs) are computed with respect to this baseline using an empirical Bayes procedure. It accounts for variation in sequencing depth by representing the logarithm of qij after accounting for size factors (sij), and it treats all samples equally by not using sample covariate information.. Role of Shrinkage: Shrinkage is applied to the LFCs for each sample relative to the baseline. Its role is to stabilize variance across the range of the mean of counts and help identify meaningful patterns in the data. However, a disadvantage is that the ordering of genes within a sample can change if neighboring genes undergo shrinkage of different strengths.. VST Comparison: Both rlog and VST are effective at stabilizing variance and are approximately equal for large counts. However, VST does not directly take into account differences in size factors, which can lead to undesirable artifacts in datasets with large variations in sequencing depth (dynamic range ≳4). Conversely, rlog has a disadvantage compared to VST in that it may change the internal ordering of genes within a sample due to variable shrinkage strengths.

## Performance Comparison

The performance of the regularized log (rlog) transformation is superior to the ordinary logarithm in terms of variance stabilization and the clarity of downstream clustering results [2]. While the ordinary logarithm—calculated as $f(K_{ij}) = \log_2(K_{ij}/s_j + 1)$—results in gene-wise standard deviations that are variable across the range of the mean of counts, the rlog transformation effectively stabilizes this variance [2]. By stabilizing variance through the range of the mean of counts, the rlog helps researchers identify more meaningful patterns in the data [2].

The impact of these transformations is evident in sample clustering [2]. Hierarchical clustering using Euclidean distances on rlog-transformed data successfully clusters samples into their appropriate treatment and time groups [2]. In contrast, using ordinary logarithm-transformed counts for the same clustering procedure produces more ambiguous results [2].

Technically, the rlog transformation is calculated by fitting a Generalized Linear Model (GLM) for each gene with a baseline expression and computing shrunken log fold changes (LFCs) [1]. It accounts for sequencing depth by representing the logarithm of $q_{ij}$ after accounting for size factors [1]. While the rlog value for large counts is approximately equal to the ordinary log of normalized counts, it offers the benefit of treating all samples equally without requiring sample covariate information [1]. However, a noted disadvantage of rlog compared to variance-stabilizing transformation (VST) is that the internal ordering of genes within a sample may change if neighboring genes undergo different strengths of shrinkage [1].

## Detailed Variance Stabilization Comparison

Based on the provided text, the comparison between the **rlog (regularized-log) transformation** and the **ordinary log transformation** (specifically $\log_2$ of normalized counts plus a pseudocount) is summarized as follows:

### **Variance Stabilization Performance**
*   **Ordinary Log Transformation:** The gene-wise standard deviation remains highly variable across the range of mean counts. Specifically, the text notes that when using the ordinary logarithm, the standard deviation is not consistent across different expression levels, leading to less reliable diagnostic results.
*   **rlog Transformation:** The rlog is significantly more effective at stabilizing variance. It results in a gene-wise standard deviation that is relatively stable across the entire range of mean counts. This stabilization allows the rlog to better reveal "meaningful patterns in the data" that the ordinary log might obscure.

### **Effect of Low Counts and Pseudocounts**
*   **Ordinary Log:** To handle counts of zero, the ordinary log requires the addition of a **pseudocount** (typically $f(K_{ij}) = \log_2(K_{ij}/s_j + 1)$). However, even with this pseudocount, the transformation fails to stabilize variance effectively, particularly for genes with low counts where the noise is more prominent.
*   **rlog:** Instead of a simple pseudocount, the rlog uses an empirical Bayes procedure to compute **shrunken log fold changes (LFCs)** with respect to a baseline expression. This shrinkage effectively moderates the noise associated with low counts. By accounting for sequencing depth ($s_{ij}$) and shrinking the LFCs, the rlog treats all samples equally without requiring the same manual adjustments as a standard log.

### **Downstream Impact (Clustering)**
The text demonstrates the superiority of rlog through hierarchical clustering on the Hammer et al. dataset:
*   **Ordinary Log:** Produced "ambiguous" clustering results where samples did not clearly group by their experimental conditions.
*   **rlog:** Successfully clustered samples into their correct groups (defined by treatment and time), proving that its variance stabilization is more robust for distance-based analyses.

## Supported Tools

At the time of the paper's publication, MultiQC supported 22 common bioinformatics tools, including aligners, processing tools, and quality control (QC) programs.

## Motivation

Next-generation sequencing studies require fast and accurate quality control (QC) [1]. Although many tools are available to quantify QC metrics, there is no standardized method to integrate this data across different tools and large sets of samples [1]. Manually evaluating analysis results for a whole project is often error-prone and time-consuming [1]. Furthermore, researchers can easily overlook outlier samples and batch effects during early analysis stages [1]. As data volumes and sample numbers increase, studies become more vulnerable to these confounding batch effects, which are often subtle and difficult to detect [1]. MultiQC was developed to address these issues by creating a single report that visualizes outputs from multiple bioinformatics tools, allowing for the rapid identification of global trends and biases [1].

## Implementation

MultiQC is a tool written in Python and executed via the command line that automates the compilation of bioinformatics quality control results [1]. It addresses the time-consuming and error-prone process of manually searching for and compiling per-sample logs from programs like FastQC, Qualimap, and RSeQC [1]. The software works by recursively scanning specified directories for recognized log files and parsing them using dedicated submodules [1][2]. As of the publication, it supports 22 common bioinformatics tools, including aligners and processing programs [2].

The primary feature of MultiQC is the generation of a single, self-contained HTML report that visualizes results across all samples [1][2]. This centralized reporting allows for shared plots, accurate comparison between samples, and the detection of batch effects [1]. For standard reports, MultiQC uses the HighCharts JavaScript library to create interactive plots that allow for zooming, resizing, and the ability to rename, hide, or highlight specific samples [2]. To maintain performance for reports containing hundreds of samples, the tool automatically switches to rendering static images using the MatPlotLib library [2].

In addition to HTML reports, MultiQC saves parsed data as YAML, JSON, or tab-delimited text for downstream applications [2]. The tool is also highly extensible; it uses code hooks and Python setuptools entry points to allow researchers to integrate custom scripts, modules, or plugins into the main program [2]. Detailed documentation and tutorial videos are provided to assist with installation and troubleshooting [2].

## Applications and Conclusion

MultiQC is designed for large-scale projects, such as single-cell and population studies, where it can parse metadata for thousands of samples in minutes [1]. The tool allows researchers to identify abnormal samples, evaluate analysis success, and use parsed data for post-processing or filtering [1]. Originally developed for high-throughput sequencing facilities, MultiQC helps staff spot failing samples and recognize irregular patterns across sample groups [1].

The software supports integration with internal systems via plugins, such as the MultiQC_NGI plugin, which connects with Laboratory Information Management Systems (LIMS) to store results and insert metadata into reports [1]. Additionally, MultiQC provides templates for report branding and generates self-contained files suitable for delivery to clients [1].

In conclusion, MultiQC automates the collection of statistics from various bioinformatics tools and provides visualizations through a simple interface [1]. It acts as a central collection point at the end of analysis pipelines, and its routine use helps mitigate risks like batch effects by facilitating early-stage quality control [1].

question: Explain how spatial heterogeneity in vaccination coverage impacts the persistence of rabies even when average coverage targets are met.
step_result_content:
## Impact of Spatial Heterogeneity on Rabies Persistence

Spatial heterogeneity in vaccination coverage—the uneven distribution of vaccinated individuals across a landscape—is a critical driver of rabies persistence [3][8]. Pockets of low vaccination coverage act as reservoirs that allow the virus to continue circulating even when district-wide average coverage might appear stable [2][8]. Research in Tanzania's Serengeti district demonstrated that major rabies outbreaks followed multi-year periods where specific clusters of villages were left unvaccinated [3][4][27]. 

The impact of this heterogeneity is significant because for the same average vaccination coverage, increased spatial variation leads to higher disease incidence [3][7]. This occurs because effective susceptibility is higher when unvaccinated dogs are concentrated in specific areas rather than being distributed evenly [6]. Furthermore, coarse data aggregated at a district level often masks these fine-scale gaps, making it difficult to identify the specific locations where transmission is maintained [2][8][11].

The study found that when spatial heterogeneity was reduced through consistent district-wide campaigns, rabies was effectively controlled, with incidence dropping to less than 0.4 cases per 1,000 dogs annually [3][8]. Notably, this control was achieved even though campaigns failed to reach the internationally recommended 70% coverage target, suggesting that minimizing spatial gaps is more vital for interrupting endemic circulation than reaching high average targets alone [2][9][40]. However, continued persistence is also driven by high population connectivity and frequent incursions from neighboring unvaccinated regions, which accounted for up to 50% of cases by 2022 [3][9][43].

## Mechanisms of Rabies Persistence via Spatial Heterogeneity

Vaccinating domestic dogs is a critical One Health intervention to prevent human rabies, yet animal vaccination programs face unique challenges compared to human programs, including faster demographic turnover and more localized movement [1]. Logistical constraints often result in vaccination coverage that is highly heterogeneous and frequently fails to meet the recommended 70% target [1][2]. This spatial heterogeneity is a significant barrier; while mass vaccination has been successful in some regions, piecemeal or inconsistent efforts in others leave populations vulnerable to disease reintroductions [2].

The impact of heterogeneity on rabies persistence is analyzed through "effective susceptibility," modeled as "power mean susceptibility" (where susceptibility equals 1 minus coverage) [8]. This approach helps explore how variations in coverage across different scales impact disease incidence [8]. Connectivity between areas is a vital factor, as rabies dynamics are driven by the interaction of local dog movements and vaccination efforts [2]. In studies of the Serengeti district, connectivity is quantified by calculating "bordering vaccination coverage" based on the proportion of borders a village shares with its neighbors [8]. Villages typically share borders with a median of five neighboring villages, making them susceptible to incursions if vaccination in adjacent areas is insufficient [4][8].

Aggregated data often fails to reflect the true risk of rabies persistence because district-wide averages can mask significant local lapses [2][5]. For example, while "campaign completeness" (the percentage of villages holding campaigns) reached 100% in the Serengeti in 2019, historical logistical constraints have frequently caused specific regions to lapse, creating spatial gaps in immunity [5]. Furthermore, high demographic turnover—with an estimated annual dog mortality rate of 44.8%—causes vaccine-induced immunity to wane rapidly at the population level [7]. Consequently, even if a district shows high average coverage, the standard deviation in village-level "rolling coverage" reveals heterogeneities that allow the virus to persist and spread [7][8].

## Workflow Requirements and Limitations

**Sarek and nf-core**
Sarek is a community-maintained workflow designed for germline and somatic variant detection that supports WGS, WES, and gene panel data [2]. Its infrastructure needs include POSIX-compatible systems, such as Linux or Mac OS X, and it is designed to operate in secure environments without direct internet access to handle sensitive personal data [2]. For rapid and easy deployment, Sarek utilizes Docker or Singularity containers [2]. 

Recent re-implementations of the nf-core/sarek pipeline using Nextflow DSL2 focus on reducing compute resources and storage requirements to allow for more efficient runs on local clusters and commercial clouds [10]. To reduce the data footprint, the workflow has transitioned to using CRAM files instead of BAM files following duplicate marking [11]. Computational efficiency is further enhanced by using updated tools like DeepVariant and DragMap, and the pipeline can be configured for specific clusters via a centralized GitHub repository of configuration files [10][11]. A primary limitation noted is the difficulty in benchmarking complex somatic variants due to a lack of robust benchmark datasets, meaning users are often referred to the tests of the individual included software components [1].

**Snakemake**
Snakemake is a text-based pipeline execution system that scales to various computational platforms and levels of parallelism [6][9]. It handles infrastructure needs by integrating with package managers like Conda and container technologies like Docker and Singularity to deploy necessary software versions automatically [5][9]. It also interacts with load-balancing software such as SLURM, Torque, and LSF for job execution [9].

For deployment and adaptability, Snakemake uses a modular approach, allowing users to include external "Snakefiles" or tool wrappers from central repositories [8]. To ensure rapid testing, it is recommended that users keep input datasets for unit tests small so they finish quickly [7]. A limitation regarding deployment is that while workflows are readable, authoring them requires specialized knowledge of Unix, Python, and the "make" utility [9]. Additionally, while declarative systems can be readable for non-developers, they may be more restrictive in the processes they can express compared to Snakemake’s integrated functional programming [5].

## Veterinary Genomic Practices and Gaps

Genomic sequencing and bioinformatics are utilized across various veterinary studies to identify, subtype, and characterize pathogens involved in disease outbreaks. In the molecular characterization of African Swine Fever Virus (ASFV) in Burkina Faso, researchers used real-time PCR and sequencing of the partial P72, complete p54, partial CD2v, and partial B602L genes to identify the virus as genotype I, serogroup 4 [1]. This sequencing allowed for the discrimination of isolates and the identification of variants based on tandem repeat sequences in the Central Variable Region (CVR) and motifs in the CD2v protein [1][2]. 

For Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) in the Netherlands, Sanger sequencing is applied to the HA cleavage site and N-subtype to provide official conformational subtyping following initial real-time PCR testing [3]. Similarly, genomic tools are used in Tanzania to integrate whole-genome sequencing with contact tracing to track the elimination of dog-mediated rabies [6]. In studies of Foot-and-Mouth Disease Virus (FMDV), deep sequencing has been used to reveal RNA sequences involved in genome packaging, while next-generation sequencing (NGS) and comparative transcriptome analysis help characterize the interactions between the virus and host cells during acute and persistent infections [7][8]. Finally, sequencing technology is described as a "crucial tool" for Lumpy Skin Disease Virus (LSDV) to examine mutations related to pathogenicity and vaccine resistance, as well as to distinguish between field strains and vaccine-derived strains through the identification of specific nucleotide insertions or deletions [9].

Regarding gaps or challenges in rapid, localized characterization, the source material notes that investigations into ASFV mortalities in Burkina Faso did not begin until two weeks after the deaths started [1]. In HPAI outbreaks, the fluctuating nature of mortality and clinical signs in certain species, such as ducks, presents a challenge for early warning; mortality thresholds used for notification were reached less often in ducks than in chickens, suggesting a need for improved clinical-sign-based early warning criteria [5]. Specific technical challenges regarding the implementation of rapid, localized genomic characterization itself were not found in the source material.

## Portable Sequencing in Veterinary Contexts

The provided content does not explicitly mention the current use or specific needs for portable sequencing technologies such as Nanopore or MinION. Instead, the documents highlight the extensive use of real-time PCR for the diagnostic confirmation and molecular characterization of various veterinary diseases. For instance, real-time PCR was used to confirm African swine fever virus (ASFV) DNA in outbreaks in Burkina Faso [1][2] and lumpy skin disease (LSD) in Nepal [4][5]. In the Netherlands, real-time PCR is used for the initial detection of highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI), followed by Sanger sequencing of the HA cleavage site for subtyping [3]. Similarly, real-time RT-PCR is utilized in gene expression studies for foot-and-mouth disease (FMD) [7]. 

Regarding mentioned needs, the research notes that FMD control is challenged by transmission that occurs before clinical signs appear, necessitating the integration of molecular and epidemiological tools to strengthen global interventions [8]. However, specific mention of "portable" or "real-time" sequencing platforms like Nanopore or MinION is not found in the source material.

## Infrastructure Requirements of Standardized Workflows

Sarek is a standardized workflow built on the Nextflow language, designed to be portable across various computational infrastructures, including high-performance computing (HPC) clusters and cloud environments [1][3]. It supports execution on HPC schedulers such as Slurm, Sun Grid Engine (SGE), LSF, and Kubernetes, as well as native support for cloud platforms including Google Cloud and Amazon Web Services (AWS) via AWS Batch [3]. The workflow can be installed on any POSIX-compatible computer system, including Linux and Mac OS X [4][16][17].

For software infrastructure, Sarek requires a local installation of Nextflow and support for at least one of three environment management systems: Docker, Singularity, or Conda [12][16][20]. Singularity is specifically noted as the preferred choice for HPC centers and environments handling sensitive personal data due to its improved security compared to Docker [16][18]. If running Sarek with Singularity, the system must also support Java 8 [19].

Regarding hardware requirements, the specific resources depend on the analysis type:
*   **Minimum Recommendations for WGS:** For a full whole-genome sequencing (WGS) analysis of a 90x/90x tumor/normal dataset, the minimum recommended specifications are 16 CPU cores, 128 GB of RAM, and at least 4 TB of free storage space [16].
*   **Storage Usage:** A benchmark 90x/90x WGS run utilized a total of 3.7 TB of storage, including temporary data [9][11][14]. Final result files (BAMs, annotated VCFs, and CNV files) accounted for approximately 1.4 TB [16]. 
*   **CPU and Efficiency:** Sarek utilizes a scatter-gather approach to distribute processing loads across CPU cores by dividing the genome into smaller chunks [12][20]. A performance test was successfully conducted using a 48-thread server (two Intel Xeon Gold 6126 CPUs) with 756 GB of memory, completing a full WGS run in approximately 48 hours [10][13][15].

## Expertise and Cost Barriers

Significant gaps exist in the technical investigation, training, and financial support required for genomic and epidemiological characterization during veterinary outbreaks. Many outbreaks are not thoroughly investigated, which results in limited available information regarding the epidemiology and molecular characteristics of disease spread [8]. While genomic sequence analysis has been utilized to identify viral lineages and cross-species exchange, there is a pressing need to better integrate molecular and epidemiological tools and to expand research beyond a narrow range of host breeds and age groups to reflect natural contexts [7][47][48][51].

Technical expertise and training gaps are evidenced by the reliance on international support; for instance, researchers in Nepal required financial support and guidance from organizations like FAO ECTAD and regional training programs in Thailand to fulfill training requirements and refine their manuscripts [1][4][11]. Furthermore, successful management of diseases like Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) is often hindered by logistical challenges and insufficient awareness, highlighting the need for enhanced training for personnel in vaccine quality control and delivery [33][36].

Financial costs present a major barrier to performing comprehensive characterizations. Investigating outbreaks is logistically challenging and expensive, particularly regarding the high cost of maintaining ruminants in high-containment facilities for the long timeframes necessary for research [46][52]. Additionally, budget and time limitations often restrict the scope and sample sizes of analytical studies during active outbreaks [12][31]. Beyond research costs, the development of preventive measures is financially demanding; for example, the need for appropriate adjuvants to improve immune responses increases the production costs of inactivated vaccines [55][58].

## Synthesis of Translation Gaps

The translation of large-scale genomic workflows like **nf-core/Sarek** into rapid, localized veterinary outbreak characterization is hindered by significant technical, temporal, and operational gaps. While these workflows provide high-quality, reproducible results for human medicine and population genetics, they are often incompatible with the immediate needs of field-based veterinary teams.

### 1. Mismatch in Computational Requirements vs. Local Infrastructure
Standardized workflows are designed for high-performance computing (HPC) or cloud environments, which are rarely available at the site of a veterinary outbreak.
*   **Intensive Resource Demands:** A single WGS analysis run via Sarek requires approximately **1790 CPU hours** and can generate over **3.7 TB** of temporary data [Chunk 19, 21]. Peak memory usage can reach **128 GB**, requiring specialized server hardware [Chunk 19].
*   **Connectivity and Deployment Barriers:** Sarek relies on the ability to pull Docker/Singularity containers from DockerHub or manage Conda environments [Chunk 22]. In many outbreak regions, such as rural Burkina Faso or Nepal, internet access may be restricted or nonexistent, making the deployment of these "portable" pipelines impossible in a localized lab [Chunk 1, 33, 41].
*   **Storage Footprint:** The storage required for results and temporary files is often three times the size of the original input data [Chunk 20]. Local veterinary diagnostic units, such as the regional labs in Nepal or Burkina Faso, may lack the data infrastructure to host such volumes [Chunk 2, 37].

### 2. Lack of Real-Time Analysis and Response Support
Large-scale workflows are optimized for comprehensive characterization rather than the "real-time" speed required to stop an escalating animal disease.
*   **Temporal Delays:** Sarek takes approximately **48 hours** to process 90X WGS data [Chunk 15, 20]. When combined with the time needed for sample transport to centralized labs, the window for effective intervention (like quarantine or movement control) often closes. Field investigations for African Swine Fever (ASF) and Lumpy Skin Disease (LSD) frequently start **two weeks** after the first mortalities, by which time the disease has already spread to neighboring municipalities [Chunk 1, 2, 38].
*   **Diagnostic Hierarchy:** Local teams prioritize rapid diagnostic confirmation (real-time PCR or ELISA) to initiate control measures [Chunk 1, 37]. Standardized genomic pipelines are often viewed as retrospective research tools for genotype/serogroup identification rather than active diagnostic aids [Chunk 1, 56].

### 3. Operational Hurdles: Expertise and Cost
The "one-size-fits-all" approach of genomic workflows creates barriers for veterinary personnel who may not have specialized bioinformatic training.
*   **Expertise Gap:** While Sarek aims to minimize management overhead, it still requires "bioinformaticians looking for an NGS analysis workflow" [Chunk 11]. In contrast, field-based veterinary services rely on local technicians and animal health workers who focus on clinical signs and basic sample collection [Chunk 30, 32]. 
*   **Financial Constraints:** Even with recent 50% reductions in cloud computing costs, these analyses remain expensive for finite veterinary budgets [Chunk 54, 56]. Local studies in Nepal specifically cited **"limitations of time and budget"** as factors in their analytical depth, which is incompatible with the high costs of cloud-scale genomic processing [Chunk 4].
*   **Maintenance Overhead:** The complexity of installing and diagnosing failed runs in a multi-tool workflow like Sarek remains high, often exceeding the actual computation time for non-experts [Chunk 11, 16].

### 4. Methodological Incompatibilities
*   **Focus on Complex Genomes:** Sarek is heavily optimized for human medulloblastoma or cancer genomes (somatic/germline variants) [Chunk 19, 54]. Rapid veterinary characterization often requires focused analysis of specific viral markers—such as the P72 or B602L genes in ASFV—which may not require a full WGS pipeline [Chunk 1].
*   **Data Fragmentation:** Veterinary surveillance systems, such as Ethiopia’s DOVAR-II, are often web-based and designed for passive reporting of cases and deaths [Chunk 6]. There is currently no seamless "translation layer" between these epidemiological reporting systems and the complex VCF outputs generated by workflows like Snakemake or Sarek [Chunk 6, 15, 52].

## bTB Prevalence Estimates

The study conducted in the South and East regions of Cameroon estimated the prevalence of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) using two primary diagnostic methods with varying thresholds:

**Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT)**
*   **Threshold of ≥3 mm:** The study found a prevalence of **6.8%** (representing 11 out of 160 cattle) [3][12][17].
*   **Threshold of ≥4 mm:** The prevalence was estimated at **0.6%** (1 out of 160 cattle) [12]. (Note: The study abstract also lists a 1.8% estimate for the 4 mm threshold [3]).

**Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT/IDT)**
*   **Threshold of 4 mm:** The prevalence was estimated at **1.8%** (3 out of 160 cattle) [12]. (Note: The study abstract also lists a 0.6% estimate for the simple IDT at this threshold [3]).

The researchers noted that applying a threshold of 3 mm significantly increased the sensitivity of bTB detection and the actual prevalence recorded compared to the 4 mm threshold recommended by the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) [17][18][26]. While the study referenced that other research in Ethiopia identified a threshold of **>2 mm** as providing the best diagnostic characteristics, that specific threshold was not used to calculate a prevalence rate for this particular study in Cameroon [24].

## Detailed bTB Prevalence Estimates

The provided text details several bovine tuberculosis (bTB) prevalence estimates for both the primary study area in South and East Cameroon and other regions globally.

**Prevalence Estimates in South and East Cameroon (Primary Study)**
*   **Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT):**
    *   At a 3mm threshold, the prevalence was 6.8% (95% CI: 4.35%–9.41%) [1][2][4][9].
    *   At a 4mm threshold, the prevalence was 0.6% (95% CI: 0%–1.2%) [1][9]. (Note: One section mentions 1.8% for a 4mm CIDT threshold, but this is later clarified as the SITT value [2]).
*   **Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT/IDT):**
    *   At a 4mm threshold, the prevalence was 1.8% (95% CI: 0%–3.6%) [1]. Another segment lists the IDT prevalence at the 4mm threshold as 0.6% (95% CI: 0%–1.2%) [2][16].

**Specific Sub-group Estimates (South and East Cameroon)**
*   **Breed:** The Goudali breed showed a prevalence of 9.16% (95% CI: 7.21%–11.27%) at the CIDT ≥3mm threshold [17]. Prevalence for Bororo, Ndama, and Simmental breeds at this threshold was 0% [17].
*   **Body Condition:** Animals with a "normal" body score had a prevalence of 19% (95% CI: 7.52%–11.3%) at the CIDT ≥3mm threshold and 17.85% (95% CI: 10.5%–27.3%) at the CIDT ≥4mm threshold [17].
*   **Age:** Cattle under 3 years old had a prevalence of 13.5% (95% CI: 10.55%–16.05%) at the CIDT ≥3mm threshold [17].
*   **Region:** The South region had an apparent prevalence of 5.33% (95% CI: 4.2%–6.8%), while the East region had 8.23% (95% CI: 5.1%–10.97%), both using the CIDT ≥3mm threshold [17][18].

**External and Historical Prevalence Estimates**
*   **Cameroon Highlands (Adamaoua and Northwest):** A previous study by Ndukum et al. found a prevalence of 5.53% (95% CI: 3.59%–7.48%) at a CIDT threshold of 3mm [9][13].
*   **Ethiopia:** 
    *   Northwest Ethiopia: 9.1% (diagnostic method not specified in text) [7].
    *   Eastern Ethiopia (dairy cows): 20.3% using CIDT at a threshold >4mm [4][7].
*   **Egypt (2020):** Prevalence in dairy cows was estimated at 68.75% (95% CI: 46%–91.4%) and 1.67% (95% CI: 1.3%–2.1%) using CIDT [7].
*   **Bangladesh:** Prevalence in dairy cows was 11.8% using CIDT [4].

## H5N1 Clade 2.3.4.4b Analysis


### Clinical Presentations and Frequency of H5N1 Clade 2.3.4.4b

**Humans:**
- **Frequency:** Extremely rare, with fewer than 10 cases identified globally as of the report date. Cases have been reported in the UK, USA, China, Vietnam, Ecuador, and Chile.
- **Clinical Presentation:** Most infections are mild or asymptomatic. However, severe cases can occur, presenting as acute febrile respiratory disease or unexplained neurological disease. Potential symptoms also include conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal issues.

**Mammals:**
- **Frequency:** High impact across a wide range of species (e.g., skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, sea lions). Notable events include significant die-offs in sea lions and the culling of thousands of mink. While severe cases are most often detected, milder disease is suspected to be prevalent but under-reported due to surveillance bias.
- **Clinical Presentation:** Predominantly severe neurological signs. Deaths are typically the result of encephalitis or meningoencephalitis. Adaptive mutations (e.g., PB2-E627K) have been found in the brains of various carnivores.


## Comparative Analysis: Mammals vs Humans

Based on the provided documents, the clinical presentations, frequency, and scale of H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b infections differ significantly between mammals and humans as follows:

### **Clinical Presentation**
*   **In Mammals:** The disease is primarily characterized by **severe neurological signs**. Most infected mammals die from **encephalitis or meningoencephalitis**. While the documents note that milder disease likely exists, surveillance is currently biased toward severely ill or dead animals.

However, the virus has the potential to cause **acute febrile respiratory disease** or **unexplained neurological disease**. Other reported symptoms (associated with H5 strains generally) include conjunctivitis and gastrointestinal distress.

*   **In Mammals:** The scale is described as a "massive scope" and an "unprecedented global outbreak." Spillover has occurred in a wide range of species, including skunks, foxes, bears, mink, seals, sea lions, and dolphins. Specific mass mortality events include:

question: What specific software and phylogenetic methods were utilized for the analysis of the ASFV sequences, and what variation was found in the Central Variable Region (CVR)?
step_result_content:
## Software and Phylogenetic Methods

The molecular characterization and phylogenetic analysis of African swine fever virus (ASFV) sequences were performed using several software packages and specific statistical methods. Raw sequences were assembled and edited using Vector NTI 11.5 software [1]. Multiple sequence alignments were conducted with MUSCLE as implemented in MEGA software version 7 [1].

For phylogenetic analysis, different methods were applied depending on the gene target:
*   **p72 gene:** A Neighbor-Joining (NJ) tree was produced using the Maximum Composite Likelihood method [8]. The dataset included 93 nucleotide sequences (398 characters), and the data were re-sampled 1,000 times using the bootstrap method [1][8].
*   **p54 gene:** A Minimum Evolution tree was constructed using the p-distance substitution model and the Close-Neighbor-Interchange (CNI) algorithm [8]. The initial tree was generated via the Neighbor-joining algorithm [8]. All positions with less than 95% site coverage were removed from the analysis, and the robustness was assessed with 1,000 bootstrap replicates [8].
*   **CD2v partial amino acid sequences:** A maximum‐likelihood (ML) tree was constructed applying the predetermined CpREV + G model [8]. This analysis also utilized 1,000 bootstrap replicates to assess tree topology robustness [8].

Additionally, the CVR nucleotide sequences were translated into amino acids, and the deduced amino acid tetramers were matched with previously reported codes for classification [11].

## CVR Variation

Molecular characterization of African Swine Fever Virus (ASFV) isolates from 2018 outbreaks in Burkina Faso involved the analysis of the Central Variable Region (CVR) within the B602L gene [2][4]. This region is defined by amino acid tandem repeats [6]. The study identified four distinct variants of the tetrameric repeat sequence (TRS) based on the number of tandem repeats: 12, 23, 24, and 32 [9][12]. To determine these variants, nucleotide sequences were translated into amino acids and matched with established tetramer codes [11].

The specific amino acid tetramer sequences for these variants were documented as follows:
*   **12 TRS Variant:** (ABNAAACBNAFA), which was found in the index outbreak at Saaba as well as in Nioko II and Kossodo [9][10].
*   **23 TRS Variant:** (ABNAAA AAA ACA AAA AACBNAFA), found in Kossodo and Tampouy [10][12].
*   **24 TRS Variant:** (AAAABNABBNABBAABBNABNABA), which was identified as a unique profile found only at the Nioko II farm [10][12].
*   **32 TRS Variant:** (ABNAAA AAC BNAAA AAC BNAAA AAA ACBNAFA), found in Kossodo and matching the isolates later collected in Tampouy [10][12].

Three of the four identified variants shared motifs that began with the tetramer "ABNAAA" and ended with "CBNAFA" [9]. The discovery of these four variants, alongside ten different variants identified in the country between 2007 and 2010, brings the total number of identified CVR variants in Burkina Faso to 14 [12].

## Genotyping and Comparative Analysis

The 2018 African swine fever virus (ASFV) isolates from Burkina Faso were identified as belonging to p72 genotype I [1][11][13]. Further molecular characterization of the E183L gene categorized these isolates into the genotype Ia subgroup [11][14]. These genotype Ia isolates comprised two distinct sub-groups based on the full length of the p54 gene, measuring either 552 bp or 564 bp [11]. Analysis of the partial CD2v gene confirmed that all sequenced isolates belong to serogroup 4 [1][11][16][22]. 

Within these 2018 outbreaks, researchers identified four variants of the central variable region (CVR) based on the number of tetrameric repeat sequences (TRS), specifically variants with 12, 23, 24, and 32 TRS [11][16]. Additionally, characterization of the CD2v amino acid sequence revealed five variants based on the number of deleted KCPPPK/KPCPPP motifs in the C-terminal proline-rich region [1][2][11]. 

When compared to historical data, a study of Burkina Faso samples collected between 2007 and 2010 identified ten CVR variants, all of which were different from the four variants found in the 2018 outbreaks [19]. This indicates a total of 14 distinct CVR variants identified in the country across these periods [19]. Historically, genotype I was the only genotype reported to be circulating in West Africa [13][14]. However, more recent data shows that genotype II has emerged in Nigeria [14]. In other African regions, Cameroon (Central Africa) reports only genotype I, while Chad and the Central African Republic have co-circulating genotypes I and IX [14]. In the Democratic Republic of Congo, genotypes I, IX, and XIV have been found to co-circulate [14][16].

question: How does the clinical impact of Lumpy Skin Disease Virus (LSDV) differ in terms of its spread within a herd versus its lethality?
step_result_content:
## Clinical Impact: Spread vs Lethality

Lumpy skin disease virus (LSDV) exhibits a high capacity for spread within a herd (morbidity) but relatively low lethality (mortality). In the 2022 outbreak in Nawalpur, Nepal, the overall morbidity rate was 28.02% [1][2][4]. The lethality of the disease was lower, with an overall mortality rate of 3.06% and a case fatality rate of 10.90% [3][4][7]. These findings are consistent with general clinical observations that morbidity rates typically range from 2% to 45%, while mortality usually remains below 10% [5].

The impact of the virus varies significantly across different animal groups:
*   **Morbidity/Spread:** Dry cattle (including pregnant cows) were the most affected group with a morbidity rate of 47.62% [2][3][4]. This was followed by cattle calves (33.33%) and heifers (32.73%) [2][3]. Buffalo showed much lower susceptibility, with morbidity rates ranging from 0% in heifers to a maximum of 4.55% in dry buffalo [3].
*   **Lethality:** The highest lethality was recorded in cattle heifers, which had a mortality rate of 5.09% and a case fatality rate of 15.56% [2][3][7]. Milking cattle followed with a mortality rate of 4.04% and a case fatality rate of 12.95% [3][7]. No deaths were recorded among any category of buffalo or male cattle during the study [3].

Comparatively, the morbidity observed in Nepal (28.02%) was similar to rates reported in Thailand (31%) and Jordan (35.1%), but higher than rates found in Bangladesh (21%), Saudi Arabia (6%), and India (7.1%) [1]. The mortality rate in Nepal (3.06%) was higher than that of Thailand (0.9%), Jordan (1.3%), and India, where no mortality was recorded in certain districts [1].

The spread of LSDV is primarily attributed to mechanical transmission by arthropod vectors like mosquitoes and flies rather than direct contact [4][10]. Analysis indicated that the presence of sick animals on neighboring farms was the most significant factor associated with a disease outbreak on a farm [4][11].

## Detailed Clinical Impact Analysis

They explicitly recommend adopting a **3 mm threshold** for the CIDT to ensure more efficient detection and to better reflect the "enzootic nature" of the disease in the region.
*   **Environmental Context:** The study suggests that defining a threshold value most suitable to the specific environmental and epidemiological context is crucial for accurate exposure assessment.

## Diagnostic Methods and Threshold Impact

The study evaluated the prevalence of bovine tuberculosis (bTB) in the South and East regions of Cameroon using two diagnostic methods: the Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT) and the Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT) [2][3][28]. Using the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) recommended threshold of 4mm, the SITT identified three positive reactions (1.8% prevalence), while the CIDT at the same threshold identified only three reactions or 0.6% prevalence [1][22][31]. question: How do the collective methodologies across Sarek, Snakemake, nf-core, and MultiQC redefine the concept of 'quality control' from a single-sample metric to a system-wide diagnostic process?
step_result_content:
## System-wide Quality Control in Sarek

Sarek is an open-source, community-maintained workflow designed for the detection, annotation, and quality control of germline and somatic variants using WGS, WES, or gene panel data [2][12][31]. By utilizing the Nextflow domain-specific language, Sarek offers a transparent and easy-to-read codebase that allows for robust portability across diverse compute environments, including cloud platforms like AWS and Google Cloud [13][24][31].

Sarek redefines quality control by moving beyond isolated single-sample metrics to an aggregated, system-wide diagnostic process. The workflow generates a comprehensive range of quality control metrics using tools such as FastQC, QualiMap, BCFtools, Samtools, and VCFtools [1][22]. These results are integrated and visualized as a unified report across all samples using MultiQC, allowing for an overview of the entire analysis run [1][11][23]. This system-wide approach is supported by Nextflow’s native error-reporting capabilities, which help diagnose software or hardware failures during execution [13][24]. Furthermore, Sarek supports the relaunching of incomplete runs from any stage, ensuring that management overhead is minimized during complex processing tasks [13][24][34].

To ensure reproducibility and ease of installation, Sarek adheres to the nf-core framework guidelines [13][24]. All software dependencies are encapsulated within Docker or Singularity containers or managed through Conda environments, which avoids the need for manual tool installation and ensures consistent performance across different POSIX-compatible systems [12][13][21][25]. This integration within the nf-core community effort ensures that Sarek remains a well-documented and community-tested solution for high-throughput genomic analysis [13][17][24].

## Nextflow as a Diagnostic Engine

Based on the provided documents, Sarek utilizes Nextflow’s native features to provide system-wide diagnostics and workflow management in the following ways:

### 1. Error Reporting and Run Diagnostics
Sarek leverages Nextflow’s ability to capture and report specific error codes from the underlying software tools. This allows for a "system-wide diagnostic" approach where the workflow can distinguish between different types of failures:
*   **Software/Hardware Diagnosis:** Nextflow reports the specific failed process and the error code from the underlying software, helping users determine if a failure was due to a software bug, corrupted data, or a hardware issue (Chunk 40, 52).
*   **Automated Error Messaging:** In response to reviewer feedback, Sarek developers improved error messages related to environment configurations (e.g., the `-profile` argument), making it easier for users to identify if a system lacks required dependencies like Singularity (Chunk 18, 41).

### 2. Checkpointing and Restarting
Unlike manual pipelines where a failure might require restarting from the beginning, Sarek utilizes Nextflow’s **checkpointing** capabilities:
*   **Stage-Independent Restarts:** Sarek is designed so that incomplete or failed runs can be easily restarted from any stage in the workflow process without re-processing successfully completed steps (Chunk 21, 52).

### 3. Resource Usage and Load Distribution
Sarek uses Nextflow to manage and report on the heavy computational demands of WGS analysis:
*   **Scatter-Gather Approach:** Sarek distributes the processing load across CPU cores by dividing the genome into smaller chunks, each handled as a separate core job. These are then merged and sorted in a final step (Chunk 4, 23).
*   **Detailed Resource Tracking:** The documentation provides specific resource usage metrics (Table 2), including CPU hours, wall clock time, and peak memory for each phase of the pipeline (Mapping, Recalibration, Variant Calling), allowing for system-level optimization (Chunk 1, 12).
*   **Cloud and HPC Integration:** Sarek utilizes Nextflow’s native support for different execution environments (Slurm, Sun Grid Engine, Kubernetes) and cloud services (AWS Batch, Google Cloud). This allows the system to distribute thousands of batch jobs across a cluster or cloud environment efficiently (Chunk 21, 52).

### 4. Environment Portability (Profiles)
Nextflow’s **configuration profiles** allow Sarek to move between different hardware systems seamlessly while maintaining a diagnostic record of the environment:
*   Users can invoke specific profiles (e.g., `-profile singularity` or `-profile conda`) which automatically manage software dependencies via Docker or Singularity containers. This ensures that the "system" remains consistent and reproducible across different compute environments (Chunk 21, 27).

### Summary: System-wide vs. Sample-level
While Sarek provides **sample-level QC** through tools like MultiQC, FastQC, and QualiMap (Chunk 3, 20), it provides **system-wide diagnostics** through Nextflow by monitoring process-level success, managing resource allocation across nodes/cores, and providing a transparent framework for debugging infrastructure-level failures.

## Cohort-Wide Aggregation with MultiQC

Based on the provided document, MultiQC functions as the final integration layer for quality control within the Sarek workflow. Here is how it transforms individual tool outputs into a collective, system-wide diagnostic report:

### 1. Integration of Diverse Metric Sources
Sarek utilizes a wide range of state-of-the-art software to generate raw quality metrics at various stages of the genomic analysis (WGS, WES, or gene panels). MultiQC acts as a centralized collector for the outputs of these specific tools:
*   **Sequence Quality:** FastQC
*   **Alignment/Mapping Stats:** QualiMap and Samtools
*   **Variant Calling Metrics:** BCFtools and VCFtools
*   **Other Metrics:** BamQC (mentioned in the software list)

### 2. Aggregation Across the Cohort
The primary mechanism of MultiQC is **aggregation**. Instead of requiring a researcher to open dozens or hundreds of individual HTML reports or log files for each sample in a cohort, MultiQC parses the data from every sample processed by the Sarek pipeline. It then compiles these disparate data points into a single, unified view.

### 3. Transformation into a "System-Wide" Review
The document notes that Sarek generates an "aggregated quality control review across samples." This transformation provides several diagnostic advantages for the entire cohort:
*   **Visual Comparative Analysis:** By visualizing metrics across all samples simultaneously, MultiQC allows users to identify outliers or systematic batch effects that might be invisible when looking at single-sample reports.
*   **Unified Reporting:** It presents a "wide range of quality control metrics" in one place, covering everything from the initial FASTQ sequence quality to the final VCF variant statistics.
*   **Scalability:** Because Sarek is designed to handle large-scale data (such as 90x coverage WGS), MultiQC’s ability to summarize results for "multiple tools and samples in a single report" (as noted in the references) is essential for maintaining data security and efficiency in high-performance computing environments.

In summary, MultiQC transforms individual, tool-specific logs into a **collective diagnostic report** by parsing the outputs of Sarek’s QC suite (FastQC, QualiMap, etc.) and synthesizing them into a single, interactive visualization that represents the entire study cohort.

## Statistical Analysis and Model Refinement

The provided documents identify several statistical software packages and metrics used to refine logistic regression models and verify the independence of risk factors across different veterinary studies.

**Statistical Software**
*   **R Software:** Version 2.10.0 was used for univariate and multivariate analyses to determine factors influencing tuberculosis status [3][9]. Version R-3.3.0 was utilized for univariate and multiple logistic regression in a study on Brucellosis [17].
*   **IBM SPSS Statistics:** Versions 20.0 and 27.0 were employed for data analysis in the Cameroon bovine tuberculosis study [3][9].
*   **STATA:** Statistical software version 14.0 was used to perform univariable and multivariable logistic regression for a study on Peste des Petits Ruminants (PPR) [15][16].
*   **Microsoft Excel 2010:** This was widely used across studies to organize and code data before analysis [3][9][15][17].

**Model Refinement Metrics**
*   **Akaike Information Criterion (AIC):** This is a primary metric for determining model quality; lower AIC values indicate a better-fitting model [3][9]. Researchers used a "top-down step-by-step" approach, deleting variables to see if the AIC decreased until the model could no longer be improved [3][9][11]. For example, one model's AIC was reduced from 85.07 to 45.83 through this process [1][5][11].
*   **Odds Ratios (OR) and Adjusted Odds Ratios (AOR):** These metrics quantify the strength of the association between specific variables and disease status [3][8][9][13].
*   **p-values:** Used to evaluate the statistical significance of associations, typically with a threshold of <0.05 [3][9][15][16].
*   **Lambda Likelihood Ratio Statistic (LRT):** This metric was also used during the selection of factors in the logistic models [2][10].

**Verification of Risk Factor Independence**
*   **Variance Inflation Factor (VIF):** This metric is used to check for multi-collinearity among predictors to ensure they are independent and to avoid model convergence [1][5][8][11][13]. 
    *   A VIF of 1 indicates no multicollinearity [1][5][11]. 
    *   A VIF of 1.8 suggests the variance of a coefficient is 80% higher due to correlation with other predictors [1][5][11].
    *   While there is no universal consensus on VIF thresholds, some researchers closely examine variables with a VIF above 2.5 [6][12]. 
    *   In the Cameroon study, the final model included factors such as forage reason, cattle herder occupation, and age, all of which had VIFs close to 1, indicating collinearity was not an issue [4][6][7][12][14].

question: Analyze how the choice of diagnostic methodology and specific assay thresholds influences the reported prevalence and epidemiological understanding of transboundary diseases.
step_result_content:
## Brucellosis Diagnostics

The study employed a cross-sectional design to estimate the prevalence of brucellosis in camels, small ruminants, and humans in the Somali pastoral region of Ethiopia [1][2]. To ensure accurate reporting, the diagnostic methodology utilized a serial testing approach [5]. Initially, serum samples were screened for anti-Brucella antibodies using the Rose Bengal Plate Test (RBPT) [4]. To improve the sensitivity of the RBPT in sheep and goats, the researchers used a modified ratio of one volume of antigen to three volumes of serum [5]. Any visible agglutination during this screening phase was considered a positive result [4].

Following the initial screening, all RBPT-positive samples underwent confirmatory testing to increase diagnostic accuracy [5]. Animal samples were tested using a commercial competitive ELISA (c-ELISA), while human samples were analyzed using an IgG ELISA [5]. The study's case definition for seropositivity required a sample to test positive on both the RBPT and c-ELISA methods [5]. Because brucellosis vaccination is not practiced in Ethiopia, this specific testing threshold allowed researchers to attribute seropositivity to natural infection [5].

Based on this methodology, the reported overall seroprevalence was 5% in small ruminants, 2.9% in camels, and 2.0% in occupationally linked humans [6]. Specifically, goats showed a higher seroprevalence of 6.5% compared to sheep at 2.0% [6]. The distribution of these results varied by district; for instance, Dolo Ado reported the highest seroprevalence in camels (3%), while Goro Baqaqsa had the highest proportion of seropositive small ruminants (6%) and humans (2.8%) [7].

## Bovine TB Diagnostics

The Comparative Intradermal Tuberculin Test (CIDT) is used to estimate the prevalence of Bovine TB (bTB) by measuring the difference in skinfold thickness variation between bovine purified protein derivative (PPD-B) and avian-PPD (PPD-A) [4][5]. The choice of cut-off points significantly influences the resulting prevalence estimates within the study population in Cameroon [7]. 

When applying the World Organization for Animal Health (WOAH) recommended threshold of >4 mm for the CIDT, the study identified only one positive animal, resulting in an apparent prevalence of 0.6% [7]. However, when the threshold was lowered to >3 mm, the number of positive reactions increased to 11, leading to a significantly higher prevalence estimate of 6.8% [7]. For comparison, the Simple Intradermal Tuberculin Test (SITT) conducted at a 4 mm threshold identified three positive reactions, yielding a prevalence of 1.8% [7]. 

The testing procedure involves intradermal injections in the cervical region, with results measured 72 hours later [4]. Statistical analysis indicated that factors such as body condition score significantly influenced the prevalence results when using the 3 mm CIDT threshold [7]. Information regarding a "doubtful" range specifically between 2-4mm for the CIDT was not explicitly detailed in the provided text beyond the negative threshold being <2mm [5].

## PPR Diagnostics

The study utilized a competitive ELISA (c-ELISA) methodology to detect antibodies against the Peste des Petits Ruminants virus (PPRV) using the ID Screen® PPR Competition ELISA kit [4]. This diagnostic tool has a reported sensitivity of 94.5% and a specificity of 99.4% [4]. The methodology involved measuring optical densities (ODs) at 450 nm and converting them into a sample negativity percentage (S/N%) using the formula: S/N % = [OD sample / OD NC] X 100 [4]. For reporting purposes, samples were classified as positive if the S/N% was 50% or less, negative if it was greater than 60%, and doubtful if the value fell between 50% and 60% [4].

The impact of this diagnostic approach on seroprevalence reporting was significant, allowing for the categorization of results based on vaccination status and risk factors [5]. The c-ELISA revealed a seroprevalence of 32.1% in non-vaccinated small ruminants and 45.5% in those with an unknown vaccination history [5][6]. Among the vaccinated population, the methodology identified a seroconversion rate of 68.8% [5][6]. 

Furthermore, the methodology enabled the identification of specific risk factors affecting seropositivity [5]. In non-vaccinated animals, factors such as older age (7.3 times more likely to be seropositive than adults), animal origin (purchased or gifted), medium flock size, and poor access to veterinary services were identified as statistically significant [5][6][7]. For vaccinated animals, the diagnostic reporting showed that goats had a 3.1 times higher probability of seroconversion than sheep, and animals in poor body condition were 5.5 times more likely to test positive for antibodies than those in good condition [7]. These findings, integrated with a five-year retrospective analysis of outbreak data from the Ministry of Agriculture, provided a comprehensive spatial and temporal view of PPR distribution across the Borena zone [1][4][7].
